periods.analysis: At 7 school safety incidents per 1,000 students, we are in yellow and sitting at the upper edge of the watch zone against a target of <=5.0. I read this quarter as a baseline, not a verdict: the first six weeks of school brought predictable pressure points at middle-school transitions, airport-corridor bus transfers, and two large high-school lunch waves. The Harborview Safe Start teams logged the heaviest concentration at Bayside Middle, Northgate High, and the Route 14/22 dismissal corridor, where supervision gaps showed up before routines were fully set. The good news is that the incidents are visible, mapped, and operationally addressable rather than diffuse across the whole system.
periods.recommendations: Hold the yellow posture and immediately tighten the first-45-days playbook: assign extra climate coaches to Bayside Middle and Northgate High, and add adult coverage to the Route 14/22 dismissal corridor. Require every principal with a rate above 7.0 to review incident time-of-day maps weekly with the safety, counseling, and transportation leads. Keep the city-school Safe Passages detail active through October rather than treating it as a launch-only support.

periods.analysis: The rate moved from 7 to 6.8 incidents per 1,000 students, a quarter-over-quarter improvement of -0.2, but it remains yellow and above the <=5.0 target. That small decline tells me the basic routines are beginning to hold, especially after staggered dismissal adjustments at Northgate High and the addition of two hall monitors at Bayside Middle. We also saw fewer bus-platform conflicts after Transportation separated Routes 14 and 22 by five minutes at Harborview Transit Center. The watch item is winter-break reentry, because short weeks, exams, and attendance volatility can quickly undo modest gains.
periods.recommendations: Continue the staggered-dismissal and transit-center separation through the first month after winter break, and do not release those supports until the data show two consecutive clean weeks. Have Student Support Services run reentry circles for the ninth-grade cohort and the three middle schools with the highest referral volume. Pair the safety review with chronic-absenteeism outreach, because disconnected students are overrepresented in preventable hallway and bus conflicts.

periods.analysis: We improved from 6.8 to 5.9 incidents per 1,000 students, a -0.9 movement and the strongest quarter-over-quarter progress in this run. We are still yellow, but this is the first quarter where the system looks like it is bending toward the <=5.0 target rather than merely managing around 7.0. The Restorative Reset rooms at Central, Bayside, and Seaport Middle appear to be reducing repeat incidents, particularly for sixth- and ninth-grade students after lunch. I am encouraged, but the watch item is consistency: a few campuses are now carrying a disproportionate share of the remaining incidents.
periods.recommendations: Lock in the practices that worked by funding the Restorative Reset rooms through the end of the school year and publishing a standard operating guide for referral, de-escalation, and return-to-class. Move one mobile behavior specialist to the three campuses still above the district yellow average for a six-week coaching cycle. Begin planning summer bridge supports for rising sixth and ninth graders so this improvement is not lost at the next transition point.

periods.analysis: The rate rose from 5.9 to 6.3 incidents per 1,000 students, a +0.4 move, so we remain yellow and have given back part of the prior quarter's progress. I am not satisfied with that reversal, but I do not see it as a systemwide breakdown; the uptick clustered around end-of-year events, substitute coverage days, and afternoon transitions at four campuses. Harborview High's temporary gym construction also compressed lunch circulation, and that produced more peer conflicts than our plan anticipated. The watch item is spring-to-summer fatigue, especially among students already flagged for chronic absenteeism and repeated minor referrals.
periods.recommendations: Run a targeted end-of-year safety sprint at the four highest-incident campuses, with assistant principals assigned to lunch, bus, and restroom hot spots instead of office coverage during peak windows. Require construction-period circulation plans at Harborview High to be reviewed weekly until the gym access issue is resolved. Use attendance and referral data to invite the highest-risk students into summer mentoring slots before they leave for break.

periods.analysis: We moved from 6.3 to 6.7 incidents per 1,000 students, another +0.4 increase, keeping us in yellow and uncomfortably close to the red threshold of >7.0. This quarter reflects the start-of-school surge we expected, but the level is higher than I want after the gains we saw earlier in 2025. The new phone-free classroom policy reduced instructional disruptions, yet some of the enforcement friction shifted into hallways during the first three weeks at East Harbor High and Mariner Middle. The watch item is adult consistency: when every adult uses the same script, incidents de-escalate; when they do not, students find the seams.
periods.recommendations: Deploy the Safe Start 2.0 coaching team to East Harbor High, Mariner Middle, and Bayside Middle for daily hallway calibration during arrival, lunch, and dismissal. Give principals a common phone-policy enforcement script and require quick audits twice a week through October. Sustain the ninth-grade advisory circles that showed promise in 2025-Q1, but extend them to include students with two or more prior safety referrals.

periods.analysis: The rate held at 6.7 incidents per 1,000 students, a 0.0 quarter-over-quarter change from 6.7, so the system is stable but still yellow and still above the <=5.0 target. Flat performance is better than sliding into red, yet it is not the improvement our students and staff deserve. The bright spot is that incident severity remained concentrated in lower-level conflicts after the Safe Start 2.0 hallway calibration, while repeat behavior at a handful of campuses continued to drive the rate. The watch item is the small group of repeat-involved students, many of whom also have attendance gaps and unfinished support plans.
periods.recommendations: Create a repeat-incident review list every Friday and require school teams to complete a support plan within five school days for any student with three incidents in the quarter. Keep Safe Start 2.0 in place at the three highest-volume campuses, but shift one coach from hallway observation to family conferences and reentry planning. Coordinate with the city youth outreach team so students with chronic absenteeism and safety referrals receive one integrated contact plan rather than separate, competing interventions.

periods.analysis: The rate improved from 6.7 to 6.1 incidents per 1,000 students, a -0.6 movement, which keeps us yellow but moves us in the right direction again. This is the kind of measured progress I trust because it followed specific operational changes: repeat-incident reviews, tighter reentry plans, and better adult coverage during lunch and dismissal. Central Middle and East Harbor High both showed cleaner weekly trend lines after adding counselor-led reentry conferences within 24 hours of a suspension or removal. The watch item is sustaining the improvement through spring activities, when assemblies, athletics, and field trips change the normal supervision pattern.
periods.recommendations: Make the Friday repeat-incident review a permanent practice through the end of the school year and require a district dashboard check every Monday morning. Pre-brief safety plans for spring assemblies, athletics, and field trips, with named staff posts for entrances, restrooms, and bus loading. Expand the 24-hour reentry conference model to every secondary campus, beginning with students returning from suspension or repeated classroom removals.

periods.analysis: The rate ticked up from 6.1 to 6.2 incidents per 1,000 students, a +0.1 movement, so we remain yellow and essentially flat after the prior quarter's improvement. I view this as a manageable warning light, not a reversal, because the increase is small and the incident pattern stayed concentrated around predictable end-of-year pressure points. Harborview High's prom week, middle-school promotion rehearsals, and substitute-heavy testing days accounted for much of the operational strain. The watch item is the fall handoff: if we do not carry the student-level plans and supervision maps forward, we will repeat the same start-of-year spike.
periods.recommendations: Before summer closeout, require each secondary principal to submit a fall safety handoff packet with hot-spot maps, repeat-incident student plans, and staffing posts for the first 20 school days. Sustain the 24-hour reentry conference model and extend it into summer programs serving rising sixth and ninth graders. Set an explicit 2026-Q3 checkpoint of moving below 6.0 incidents per 1,000 students, with weekly review of any campus trending above the district rate.

periods.analysis: Safety incidents eased from 6.2 to 6.0 per 1,000 students. That is an improvement, but the rate remains above the target of 5.0 per 1,000.
periods.recommendations: Keep first-term supervision maps and repeat-incident plans under weekly review, especially at campuses above the district rate.
